title: Impersonal and passive se
why: Where English uses a generic “you,” “people,” “they” or a passive (“Spanish is spoken here”), Spanish uses se + verb: this lesson shows how, with plural agreement in ads (se venden pisos), plus uno and la gente. It also explains expressions you've already met (no se oye, se ha cortado) and lets you describe customs and rules.

Se + verb: Spanish's generic “you”

To talk about people in general, English says “you,” “people,” “they” or “one,” or uses a passive. Spanish's favorite tool is se + verb in the 3rd person.

EnglishSpanish
In Spain, people have dinner late.En España se cena tarde.
You eat well here.Aquí se come bien.
How do you say “window” in Spanish?¿Cómo se dice «window» en español?
They say this restaurant is very good.Se dice que este restaurante es muy bueno.
Life is good in this village.En este pueblo se vive bien.

You already know two expressions of this kind from phone calls: No se oye bien (I can't hear well) and Se ha cortado (it got cut off). The se works in every tense: Antes se trabajaba los sábados (people used to work on Saturdays).

Other ways to say it

  • La gente + singular verb: La gente cena tarde. Careful: la gente is singular in Spanish, unlike English “people”: la gente es, never “la gente son.”
  • The 3rd person plural, with no subject, when you don't know who: Dicen que va a llover. (They say it's going to rain.)
  • Uno (or una) + 3rd person, like English “one,” required when the verb is already reflexive, since “se se” is impossible: En verano uno se acuesta tarde.

Avoid using nosotros for people in general: Aquí se habla español (Spanish is spoken here), not “aquí hablamos español,” which means “we (specifically us) speak Spanish here.”

", "

Se venden pisos: plural agreement

When the verb has an object (what's being sold, what's wanted…), it agrees with that noun: singular if the noun is singular, plural if it's plural. It works like an English passive (“apartments are sold”). This is the rule for ads and signs.

SingularPlural
Se vende piso.
(Apartment for sale.)		Se venden pisos.
(Apartments for sale.)
Se alquila habitación.
(Room for rent.)		Se alquilan habitaciones.
(Rooms for rent.)
Se busca camarero.
(Waiter wanted.)		Se necesitan camareros.
(Waiters wanted.)
Se habla inglés.
(English spoken.)		Se hablan varios idiomas.
(Several languages spoken.)

The trap: writing “se vende pisos.” Look at the noun that follows: pisos is plural, so se venden. With a verb that has no object (se vive bien, se cena tarde), the verb stays singular.

Rules: se puede, no se puede

To say what's allowed or forbidden, use se puede + infinitive:

Aquí no se puede fumar.You can't smoke here.
¿Se puede pagar con tarjeta?Can I pay by card?
En esta calle no se puede aparcar.You can't park on this street.

On signs, you'll also see Prohibido fumar (no smoking) and the set phrase Se ruega silencio (silence, please).

", "

Customs in Spain

Impersonal se is perfect for talking about a country's customs. Here are a few that everyone will describe to you this way:

SpanishEnglish
Se come entre las dos y las tres y se cena hacia las diez.People have lunch between two and three and dinner around ten.
Para saludar, se dan dos besos.To say hello, people give two kisses on the cheek.
En Navidad se come turrón.At Christmas, people eat turrón (nougat).
Después de comer, se hace la sobremesa.After a meal, people stay at the table to chat.
En los bares se deja poca propina.In bars, people leave a small tip.
En Granada, con cada bebida se pone una tapa.In Granada, they serve a tapa with every drink.

Notice the agreement: se dan dos besos (plural, because of besos), but se come turrón (singular).

In the past

To compare with the old days, the imperfect is ideal, like English “used to”: Antes se trabajaba los sábados por la mañana. En mi pueblo se vivía de la agricultura. Antes no se usaba tanto el móvil.

La sobremesa has no equivalent in English: it's the time, often long, when people stay at the table after a meal to chat. And on Sundays, se come en familia.
